stories.title: Minister of Agriculture and Refugees International Discuss Food Security and El Niño Preparedness
stories.description: MOGADISHU — The Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation of the Federal Government of Somalia, Mohamed Abdi Hayir (Maareeye), has received a delegation from Refugees International (RI), led by the organization’s President, Jeremy Konyndyk, and Abdullahi Halakhe, to discuss strengthening cooperation on food security, community resilience, and agricultural investment for the recovery of livelihoods and durable solutions for displaced populations. The meeting, held at the Ministry’s headquarters in Mogadishu, focused on the importance of investing in agriculture to support the recovery of livelihoods and provide lasting solutions for internally displaced persons (IDPs). The delegation from Refugees International, a global humanitarian organization that advocates for the rights and protection of refugees and displaced people, explored ways to deepen collaboration with Somalia’s agricultural sector. The Federal Government has been actively engaging with international partners to boost food security and resilience, particularly in the face of recurring climate shocks and displacement crises. El Niño Preparedness and Climate Resilience A significant portion of the discussions was dedicated to preparedness for the anticipated El Niño weather phenomenon, which is expected to bring heavy rains and potential flooding later this year. The talks addressed the risks of floods, excessive rainfall, crop damage, and community displacement. Minister Maareeye emphasized the importance of early warning systems, water management, irrigation, and climate-resilient agriculture to mitigate the impact of disasters and protect agricultural production. The government has been coordinating with health partners on El Niño response, with SoDMA and the UN bolstering joint efforts against the escalating climate crisis. Minister Maareeye highlighted the need to invest in irrigation infrastructure and climate-smart farming techniques to reduce the vulnerability of agricultural communities to climate-related shocks. The meeting also discussed the importance of strengthening value chains, improving rural infrastructure, and creating employment opportunities for youth and women in the agricultural sector. stories.title: Researchers use reduced graphene oxide electrodes to build a compact electrically tunable soft lens
stories.description: Researchers at Queen Mary University of London, led by Prof. James Busfield, have developed transparent electrodes made of reduced graphene oxide (rGO) for dielectric elastomer actuators (DEAs), enabling a new compact, electrically tunable soft lens. The work addresses a long-standing design constraint in electrostatically actuated lenses, where opaque compliant electrodes have to be placed around the lens periphery rather than on the optical path itself. A photo of the fabricated DEA actuator (the rGO-coated membrane with circular electrodes). Image from: Advanced Functional MaterialsDEAs are soft electromechanical transducers that behave like artificial muscles: a dielectric elastomer membrane sandwiched between compliant electrodes contracts in thickness and expands laterally when an electric field is applied. They're being explored for tunable lenses, adaptive filters, camouflage skins and other electrically reconfigurable optical devices. Most implementations, however, rely on non-transparent electrodes, forcing a separate actuation ring around the lens body and increasing the device's footprint. Transparent compliant electrodes remove that constraint by letting the electrode sit directly on the optical axis. The team spray-coated a pre-stretched acrylic elastomer membrane (VHB 4905) with an rGO ink dispersed in THF, building electrodes at surface densities between 0.10 and 0.17 µg/mm² (roughly 50-80 nm thick). Raising the rGO density from the low to the high end of that range dropped the sheet resistance from about 600 to 15 kΩ/sq, but also cut optical transmittance at 550 nm from about 42% to 17% - illustrating the familiar trade-off between conductivity and transparency in thin conductive coatings, quantified here with a Haacke figure of merit.For the lens demonstration, the researchers selected a surface density of 0.12 µg/mm², balancing roughly 32% transmittance against an area strain of about 10% at a driving field of 50 V/µm. The rGO-coated DEA was bonded to a 12.5 mm-wide plano-convex PDMS lens; applying voltage radially stretches the lens and increases its focal length, shifting the focus point across a 30-36 mm range in their prototype. Because the transparent electrode sits directly on the lens rather than around it, the whole assembly keeps a compact form factor.
